label: Quadratic Equations
overview: A quadratic equation has the form ax² + bx + c = 0 and can have 0, 1, or 2 real solutions. SAT questions ask you to solve by factoring, by the quadratic formula, or by completing the square, and to use the discriminant to determine the number of solutions. Choosing the fastest method for each problem is key.

keyFormulas.name: Vertex form
keyFormulas.latex: f(x) = a(x - h)^2 + k \quad \text{(vertex at }(h, k))

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting the ± — writing only one solution from the quadratic formula
commonMistakes.fix: The ± gives two separate solutions. Always compute both +√ and −√ cases.

commonMistakes.mistake: Computing −b incorrectly when b is already negative
commonMistakes.fix: If b = −3, then −b = −(−3) = +3. Double-check the sign of −b before substituting.

quickTip: Try factoring first (it's faster). Use the quadratic formula as a fallback when factoring isn't obvious. Check the discriminant quickly to see if solutions even exist.
